Package frc.robot.subsystems

Class SubsystemBase

java.lang.Object
edu.wpi.first.wpilibj2.command.SubsystemBase
frc.robot.subsystems.SubsystemBase
All Implemented Interfaces:
edu.wpi.first.util.sendable.Sendable, edu.wpi.first.wpilibj2.command.Subsystem, Subsystem, AutoCloseable
Direct Known Subclasses:
AbstractArmSubsystem, AbstractElevatorSubsystem
public abstract class SubsystemBase extends edu.wpi.first.wpilibj2.command.SubsystemBase implements Subsystem, AutoCloseable
Base class for the concrete mechanism implementations in this library.

Robot code never extends this; it holds a mechanism interface. This class exists for the one implementation of each mechanism so that loop bookkeeping, thread safety, and goal tracking are written once rather than per mechanism. It extends WPILib's SubsystemBase, so mechanisms defined here work with the command-based framework and register with the scheduler exactly like any other subsystem.

What a subclass must supply

  • periodicImpl() — one iteration of the mechanism's control loop.
  • stopImpl() — drop outputs to a safe state.
  • closeImpl() — release the mechanism's IO.
  • SubsystemBase.getName() — a stable name for logging.
  • Subsystem.isReal() — whether this mechanism drives hardware.

Loop ordering

periodic() runs beforePeriodic(), periodicImpl(), then afterPeriodic(). The hooks exist so a subclass can do work that must not hold the state lock, such as publishing telemetry. They default to doing nothing.

Goal tracking

atGoal() is backed by a single flag the subclass sets through setGoalReached(boolean). Keeping it here means every mechanism reports goal state the same way, and a caller can sequence mechanisms without knowing how each one decides it is done.

Testability

Nothing here touches hardware, so a subclass built over a simulated IO runs unchanged in a test process. loopCount() gives tests a deterministic stand-in for elapsed time instead of a wall clock.

      public final boolean isClosed()

      true once this mechanism has been closed

    • periodicImpl

      protected abstract void periodicImpl()
      Runs one iteration of the mechanism's control loop.

      Called with the state lock held. Implementations read inputs, compute an output, and apply it to their IO. This must stay cheap — it runs every loop.

    • stopImpl

      protected abstract void stopImpl()
      Drops the mechanism's outputs to a safe state.

      Called with the state lock held, and expected to be safe at any time, including before a goal has ever been set. Implementations must not throw.

    • closeImpl

      protected abstract void closeImpl()
      Releases the mechanism's IO.

      Called once, after stopImpl(). Implementations should tolerate being handed an IO that is already closed.

    • beforePeriodic

      protected void beforePeriodic()
      Hook run immediately before periodicImpl(), outside the state lock.

      For cheap, lock-free work such as timestamping. Defaults to doing nothing.

    • afterPeriodic

      protected void afterPeriodic()
      Hook run immediately after periodicImpl(), outside the state lock.

      For telemetry that must not hold the state lock. Defaults to doing nothing.

    • setGoalReached

      protected final void setGoalReached(boolean reached)
      Records whether the mechanism has reached the goal it was commanded to.

      Subclasses call this from periodicImpl() with their own tolerance check.

      Parameters:
      reached - true if the current goal has been satisfied

    • atGoal

      public final boolean atGoal()
      Description copied from interface: Subsystem
      Returns whether the mechanism has reached the goal it was most recently commanded to.

      Used by robot code to sequence mechanisms and by tests to assert a command completed. A mechanism with no active goal reports true.

      Specified by:
      atGoal in interface Subsystem
      Returns:
      true if the mechanism is at its goal and has nothing left to do

    • loopCount

      public final long loopCount()
      Returns the number of completed loop iterations.

      A deterministic stand-in for elapsed time: driving a simulation exactly n loops makes a test reproducible regardless of how fast the machine is.

      Returns:
      the number of times periodic() has completed
